tldr: This paper demonstrates that distributing multiple miniature Time-of-Flight (ToF) sensors—costing only about $10 each—can replace expensive, power-hungry depth cameras to achieve practical close-range obstacle avoidance and footstep planning on a quadruped robot.
hero_caption: Eight low-cost ToF sensors are distributed across the front of the ANYmal D quadruped robot to sense the near-field environment around its feet. Despite their low resolution, they build local elevation maps in real time, enabling safe footstep selection and obstacle avoidance.
overview:
For quadruped robots traversing rough terrain, close-range perception that accurately captures the ground near their feet is indispensable. Depth cameras such as the Intel RealSense have been the standard choice. However, their bulky form factor makes them hard to mount near robot joints or on curved shells, inevitably creating blind spots right around the feet. High power consumption and cost have also been persistent issues.

To tackle this, the authors turned to low-cost miniature Time-of-Flight (ToF) sensors. They distributed eight multi-zone ToF sensors ($8 \times 8$ pixels), each costing just around $10$ with minimal weight and power draw, across the front shell of an ANYmal D robot to eliminate blind spots.

Although an individual sensor is noisy and ultra-low resolution, the authors combined their overlapping fields of view through careful geometric placement and integrated them into an elevation mapping pipeline matched to the robot's motion, successfully recovering practical near-field terrain.

Through 3D reconstruction accuracy evaluations using LiDAR as ground truth, footstep planning experiments across railway ties and stairs, and obstacle avoidance navigation in both simulation and the real world, they confirmed that locomotion traversal and local avoidance performance are nearly on par with conventional depth cameras. This highly practical study clearly shows that clever distributed placement can yield sufficient perceptual performance without relying exclusively on high-end sensors.
contributions: Achieved near-field perception comparable to conventional depth cameras (~$400) at dramatically lower cost and power consumption by distributing multi-zone ToF sensors costing around $10 each.

Optimally arranged eight ToF sensors across the front shell of ANYmal D, securing a wide field of view of $180^\circ$ horizontal and $90^\circ$ vertical down to the immediate vicinity of the feet, which were blind spots for traditional depth cameras.
Quantitatively evaluated indoor 3D shape reconstruction accuracy against LiDAR reference data, revealing that even coarse ToF point clouds can reliably capture structures on the order of 10 cm.

Demonstrated on real hardware that ToF-based local elevation maps achieve locomotion success rates on par with depth cameras when climbing irregular stairs, traversing railway ties, and autonomously avoiding complex obstacle courses.

sections.heading: Can Cheap ToF Sensor Arrays Replace Expensive Depth Cameras?
sections.summary: Depth cameras commonly used for close-range perception on quadrupeds suffer from blind spots, high power draw, and high cost. This work explores whether distributing miniature, inexpensive ToF sensors across a robot's exterior can eliminate near-field blind spots while enabling practical locomotion and local obstacle avoidance.
sections.details:
Quadruped robots are expected to operate in unstructured, harsh environments such as inspection tasks, disaster zones, and forest surveys. To carry out these tasks autonomously, geometric perception that accurately captures the surrounding terrain is essential.

Current mainstream platforms combine LiDAR and depth cameras, but each has weaknesses. While LiDAR excels at long-range measurement, it struggles at close range and frequently misses fine terrain features directly beneath the feet. On the other hand, depth cameras (such as the RealSense D435i) are roughly 9 cm wide and difficult to mount near robot joints or curved outer shells, inevitably creating blind spots right where the feet step. Furthermore, deploying multiple units sharply increases power consumption, computational load, and overall system cost.

This motivated the authors to explore recently advancing multi-zone Time-of-Flight (ToF) sensors. These miniature sensors measure distances to multiple points simultaneously using the round-trip time of light, costing only around $10 per unit. While a single sensor offers low resolution and notable noise, the authors hypothesized that distributing them across the robot body with overlapping fields of view would eliminate blind spots and provide sufficient information.

In this paper, eight ToF sensors are integrated onto the front of the ANYbotics ANYmal D quadruped robot, thoroughly benchmarking terrain mapping, footstep planning, and obstacle avoidance against conventional depth cameras and high-precision LiDAR.

sections.heading: The Evolution of Geometric Perception and Near-Field Sensing for Quadrupeds
sections.summary: Perception for quadruped robots has centered around LiDAR for global mapping and depth cameras for local mapping. While miniature ToF sensors have recently been adopted on drones and manipulators, whether they can support the complex footstep planning and elevation mapping required by quadrupeds has remained an open question.
sections.details:
### II-A Geometric Perception for Quadrupeds
LiDAR and depth cameras have become standard geometric sensors for quadruped robot locomotion control and path planning. LiDAR has driven large-scale state estimation and mapping in underground exploration and forest surveys. Depth cameras, meanwhile, provide dense near-field point clouds, making them popular for generating local elevation maps for model predictive control or reinforcement learning controllers to select foot placements, as well as for obstacle avoidance navigation. Recently, approaches feeding raw depth images directly into neural networks for agile maneuvers like parkour have emerged, but they still rely heavily on bulky depth cameras.

### II-B Close-range Perception
For close-range obstacle detection, single-beam ultrasonic sensors and tactile whiskers have been investigated in the past. However, ultrasonic sensors require flat-ground assumptions, and whiskers provide no information until right before contact, making both poorly suited for rough-terrain locomotion.

In recent years, due to their ultra-compact, lightweight, and low-power nature, ToF sensors have increasingly been used for collision avoidance on nano-drones. Attempts have also been made to array ToF sensors on robot arms and snake robots for proximity control. However, these applications primarily use them to obtain rough distance estimates; whether low-resolution ToF can handle demanding tasks required by quadrupeds—such as constructing precise local elevation maps to compute safe footholds in real time—had not been tested.

sections.heading: Hardware and Software Design for Distributed Low-Cost ToF Sensing
sections.summary: Eight miniature ToF sensors from STMicroelectronics were distributed across a custom front shell on ANYmal D. The system achieves fast readouts via an I2C daisy chain and integrates into an elevation mapping framework tailored to ToF noise characteristics.
sections.details:
### III-A ToF Sensors
The authors selected the VL53L5CX multi-zone ToF sensor from STMicroelectronics. Measuring an ultra-compact $6.4 \times 3.0 \times 1.5\,\mathrm{mm}$, it provides $8 \times 8$ (64 zones in total) distance measurements over a $0.02\,\mathrm{m}$ to $4\,\mathrm{m}$ range within a $65^\circ$ diagonal field of view. At about $10 each, it is dramatically cheaper than the roughly $400 RealSense D435i. Power consumption is also kept to roughly 0.2–0.4 W per unit, about one-tenth that of depth cameras (2–4 W).

### III-B ANYmal Integration
The front shell of ANYmal D was custom 3D-printed to embed the eight ToF sensors. Adjacent fields of view (FoVs) intentionally overlap partially to increase measurement density and improve robustness to noise. Simultaneously, sensor angles were carefully adjusted so the robot's own legs and body do not enter the FoV and obstruct measurements. This achieves an extremely wide coverage of $180^\circ$ horizontal and $90^\circ$ vertical, substantially covering the blind spots directly beneath the feet present in existing depth camera setups.

### III-C Software Integration
The eight sensors are daisy-chained via an I2C bus, and data is gathered via serial communication through an RP2350 microcontroller. Reading all sensors takes about 1 ms per cycle, publishing ROS 2 point cloud messages at 15 Hz. The resulting point clouds are integrated at 40 Hz into the local elevation mapping framework by Fankhauser et al., widely used on quadruped robots. To account for ToF-specific noise, parameters from the sensor error model by Nguyen et al. were adjusted and applied. The sensor data is used exclusively for elevation map generation; the robot's state estimation is handled by an onboard fusion estimator combining LiDAR odometry and proprioception.

### III-D Handheld Mapping Device Integration
To evaluate the geometric reconstruction performance of the ToF sensors alone fairly, the authors also built a handheld scanning device featuring eight ToF sensors arranged in a ring on top of a 360° Hesai PandarQT-64 LiDAR.

sections.heading: Three-Stage Validation: Reconstruction, Footstep Planning, and Avoidance
sections.summary: The system was evaluated through 3D reconstruction accuracy against LiDAR, footstep planning across ties and stairs, and autonomous obstacle avoidance in simulation and reality. Despite low resolution and noise, it demonstrated locomotion performance on par with depth cameras.
sections.details:
### IV-A Exp 1 – Reconstruction Accuracy with a LiDAR Reference
Using the handheld device, an office environment (4 m × 5 m) was scanned, using point clouds from the 64-layer LiDAR as ground truth to evaluate ToF reconstruction accuracy. Nearest-neighbor Euclidean distance calculations showed a median error of under 2 cm, successfully capturing the contours of furniture items around 10 cm in size. Comparing mesh reconstruction methods (Poisson, Ball Pivoting, TSDF) confirmed that TSDF and Poisson can reconstruct smooth, continuous room surfaces even from coarse point clouds.

### IV-B Exp 2 – Footstep Planning
Next, using the physical ANYmal D, walking performance was evaluated by feeding the ToF-generated local elevation map into a perceptual reinforcement learning (RL) controller. Baselines were maps from two front RealSense depth cameras and blind walking without exteroceptive perception. Three environments were tested:
- **Railway ties (three beams, ~13 cm high)**: Traversed at a forward speed of 40 cm/s. Blind walking tripped and failed all 3 out of 3 trials, whereas both the ToF setup and depth camera setup succeeded 10 out of 10 times.
- **Irregular indoor stairs (step heights: 9 cm, 17 cm, 17 cm)**: Blind walking collided after clearing only the first step, but both ToF and depth cameras cleared ascending and descending in all 10 trials.
- **Outdoor stairs (7 steps, 15 cm high)**: While depth cameras produced cleaner maps, the ToF's coarser map still adequately captured the step structure for foothold placement, achieving 10 out of 10 successful climbs.

### IV-C Exp 3 – Obstacle Avoidance
Finally, obstacle avoidance navigation was evaluated in combination with a local planner.
In simulation, incorporating a distance-dependent Gaussian noise model ($d_{\text{sim}} = d_{\text{GT}} + \mathcal{N}(0, (0.01 d_{\text{GT}})^2)$), courses of varying difficulty were tested. Travel distance did not differ noticeably from depth cameras, and all courses were cleared with only slightly longer durations due to minor deceleration during avoidance maneuvers. Sensor failure tests showed high fault tolerance: randomly removing sensors from the eight available caused virtually no drop in success rate with two failed sensors (six remaining), with performance degrading on hard courses only after three failed.

Real-world experiments evaluated cardboard box courses at three difficulty levels (Easy, Medium, Hard). Because ToF point clouds are coarse, the robot's legs brushed obstacles slightly more often when passing close to edges than with depth cameras, yet it reliably detected major obstacles and reached the goal. Except for stops caused by local minima in the planner (where attractive and repulsive forces balanced out), practical autonomous avoidance capability was firmly demonstrated.

captions.F5: Comparison of accumulated point clouds in an office environment. Compared to the LiDAR point cloud on the left, the point cloud from the eight ToF sensors on the right is less dense but clearly captures major indoor structures such as walls, tables, and shelves.
captions.F7: Footstep planning experiment stepping over 13 cm railway ties. The bottom row shows elevation maps generated from depth cameras (left) and the ToF array (right), confirming that ToF provides sufficient accuracy for the controller to recognize obstacle heights for foot placement.
captions.F8: Experiment climbing indoor stairs with irregular step heights. Compared to the depth camera (bottom left), the ToF elevation map (bottom right) is coarser with visible artifacts, but preserved step edge structures allowed the RL controller to climb and descend without a single misstep.

sections.heading: Summary and What Lies Ahead
sections.summary: This study showed that a low-cost distributed ToF sensor array is fully practical for quadruped footstep planning and close-range obstacle avoidance. Despite resolution limits, it is highly promising as a lightweight, low-power near-field perception modality complementary to long-range sensors.
sections.details:
This study investigated whether distributed multi-zone ToF sensors can serve as an alternative to depth cameras for near-field quadruped perception. Experimental results confirmed that while the generated elevation maps are low in resolution and contain noise, they provide sufficient geometric information for footstep planning and local navigation in cluttered environments. This enables dramatic reductions in cost, power consumption, and spatial footprint compared to traditional depth camera configurations.

Of course, limitations exist. Coarse resolution limits detection accuracy for thin wires, small obstacles, or extreme environments requiring millimeter-level foothold selection. Therefore, this ToF sensor array does not entirely replace high-precision, long-range LiDAR; rather, it is best positioned as a complementary near-field perception device that covers blind spots around the feet to safeguard close-range movement. Future work will explore multimodal fusion with other sensors and optimization of distributed placement patterns across the entire robot body.

takeaways: Distributing multiple multi-zone ToF sensors costing around $10 each can replace expensive depth cameras for close-range terrain perception on quadruped robots.

For near-field tasks using sequentially updated local elevation maps (such as footstep planning and local avoidance), centimeter-level accuracy is sufficient without needing millimeter-level resolution.
A distributed array configuration substantially eliminates hardware blind spots and exhibits high fault tolerance, preventing perceptual breakdown even if one or two sensors fail.
Dividing roles between long-range, high-precision LiDAR and low-cost, ultra-low-power distributed near-field ToF is a highly rational sensing architecture for legged robots.
limitations: Because each sensor has an extremely low resolution of only 8×8 pixels, thin poles, table legs, and small protrusions are easily missed.
Reconstructed geometries tend to round off near the edges of walls and obstacles, causing the robot's legs to brush obstacles more frequently than with depth cameras in tight spaces.
The system cannot be used for global mapping or long-range state estimation, making another perception modality such as LiDAR essential for high-level navigation.
